We've conducted a comprehensive study of fast radio bursts (FRBs) focusing on their optical behavior. By analyzing a dataset of 100 FRBs with the most precise localization techniques from the CHIME/FRB project between 2020 and 2022, we established lower bounds for their optical brightness between the z = 0.2 and z = 2 galaxy. Our research discovered that most FRBs fall below the upper limits set by the Chandra X-ray Observatory's sensitivity, with a few exceptions possibly experiencing delayed ejections of high-energy particles. Furthermore, we observed that persistent emission from FRBs is unlikely to exceed the millijansky flux density threshold. These findings are consistent with the radio burst's short duration and a variety of emission models. However, if the emission is delayed and less energetic, it could be masked by the Chandra's sensitivity threshold, with the exception of the lowest luminosity FRBs.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the standard for high-energy particle physics and materials research the past few decades, despite inherent inefficiencies and technical limitations. This study presents a model for optimizing amplifier performance, incorporating the interplay of beam parameters, gain, and threshold limits. It also reverse-engineers the Large Heavy Ion Laser System (LHILS), a proposed high-powered laser source, to enable reliable design and comparison with established systems.

Multimodal language generation models can now be controlled by non-verbal inputs like images, thanks to recent breakthroughs. Our work explores direct image featurs manipulation in T5-based models through an attention-weighted image loss technique, allowing for controlled text generation via "prompt engineering". Our method also allows us to combine text and image inputs in a single prompt, making it easier to implement and train. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach across various image-text alignment tasks, demonstrating its ability to produce high-quality and semantically accurate outputs when given image features as a cue.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme encompasses an innovative public key compression technique, a customised RingCT encapsulation process, and a method of combining public and subgroup indices with unique characteristics.
Notably, DelegCT enables the use of public keys derived from subgroups in its transactions, presenting an opportunity for enhanced anonymity when transactions involve multiple subgroups.
Furthermore, DelegCT's implementation in the Conda blockchain demonstrates a substantial 90% reduction in transaction size compared to traditional RingCT, with transaction speeds increasing by 10 times.
In contrast to other anonymity-enhancing cryptocurrencies, DelegCT's performance is also comparable to that of Bitcoin, with transaction verification occurring at a speed of 100 milliseconds.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning technique at a rate of one every ten minutes for LHC experiments, effectively utilizing full-power conditions to monitor and regulate beam properties. As a result, the LHC circulated beams at increasingly higher levels, with an ultimate goal of achieving higher luminosity for future experiments. To achieve this goal, the LHC must demonstrate the ability to accurately regulate its beam intensity through separate scans, in addition to regular delivery. To ensure smooth operation, the LHC team conducts regular separate scans three times a week, outside of regular delivery times, to maintain separation scanning capability. To address potential concerns to maintain delivery consistency, the LHC team implemented separate scanning protocols, separating production from physics delivery. To guarantee safety and minimize disruption, the LHC team scheduled separate scanning outside of production and physics delivery periods, immediately following or preceding these times. To achieve this goal, the LHC team collaborated with the CMS and ALICE experiments, obtaining essential feedback and input from the experiments to ensure separate scanning compatibility with beam injection, extraction, and regular schedules. To apply emittance scans to actual beam conditions, the LHC team introduced new emittance scan tools, separating production and physics delivery, and introduced the concept of "luminosity scans," combining emittance and beta functions into a single tool to ensure accurate beam regulation. To apply this concept to actual beam conditions, the LHC team demonstrated the first luminosity scan

To address the challenge of developing accurate models from limited data, researchers have proposed cooperative modeling - an innovative approach where multiple agents establish correlations between input and output data. By sharing their findings, these agents can collectively enhance the accuracy of their predictions, demonstrating potential solutions to data scarcity issues. This study provides a general framework for cooperative modeling based on graph theory, along with a framework for agent interaction and simulation. We evaluate the performance of this framework through theoretical analysis and case studies on both synthetic and real-world datasets, revealing its ability to surpass individual models in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our research indicates that agent accuracy is not the sole determining factor for overall performance and that our method can produce results comparable to random forest, shallow neural networks, and even outperform deep learning models on specific tasks.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ belongs to a typical bottomonium or a novel $4S-4D$ mixed state.
However, our findings suggest that these decay processes are difficult to induce
as they involve small loop amplitudes or are heavily suppressed by Clebsch-Gordan
coefficients. Therefore, our research does not fully verify the $\Upsilon(10753)$
particle.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique for training neural networks with quantized weights to reduce computational costs at inference time. We develop a method, AskewSGD, which iteratively refines search spaces and directions of descent. We derive symmetrical search spaces around each weight, narrowing them at each iteration. Similarly, we obtain symmetrical gradient vectors with the AskewSGD rule, which is derived from the negative gradient direction. We demonstrate that our method converges to the optimal solution of the quantized problem. We show that our method converges at a rate of $O(1/n)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ for convex and non-convex problems, respectively. We also derive bounds for the expected value and variance of the AskewSGD update. We compare our method with existing approaches and demonstrate its effectiveness.

The development of innovative healthcare technologies has been hindered by conventional hard-bodied robots, leading to increased interest in soft robot solutions.  These innovative systems, composed of elastic materials and employed in the shape of soft entities, can be used both as materials and devices.  Currently, they are primarily utilized in prototypical applications due to ongoing difficulties in design, modeling, and control.  This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the current state of model-based control systems for these robots, highlighting the various modeling approaches, challenges, and solutions, as well as discussing existing algorithms and their limitations in detail.  By identifying and exploring the obstacles to model-based control systems, this paper aims to lay the groundwork for the development of novel methodologies that can effectively integrate theory and practice in this field.

The Jacobi group $G_J(\mathbb{R})$ is defined by combining the group of affine transformations on the real line with a specific non-abelian group, and its irreducible infinite-dimensional representations have been extensively analyzed in existing literature. Focusing on the subset of representations that can be characterized by specific, often restrictive properties, this text revisits this area of representation theory. By distinguishing between two types of representations - those that can be broken down into the representations of two separate groups and those that cannot - this text establishes a fundamental distinction within the domain. For each type, it develops fundamental theorems that address representation creation, multiplication, and decomposition, and demonstrates how these can be used to obtain specific, often sought-after representations. By applying these theorems, this text shows how to construct specific, useful representations of the Jacobi group, and it establishes a relationship between two distinct groups of transformations - affine and Sturmian - that cannot be broken down further.

Verifying facts using tables is essential for understanding the meaning of data, but current neural system performances are hindered by state-of-the-art natural language processing systems that sometimes confirm false information. To address this issue, a new approach called TAFIS has been developed to validate fact verification using tables by leveraging multi-head attention and decomposition methods to enhance reasoning accuracy. Specifically, TAFIS employs column and row attention decomposition to pinpoint key information in tables, and column decomposition to identify the most relevant columns when information is missing. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of TAFIS in combining table and knowledge graph knowledge, and its superiority over existing systems.

The state of the art in learning probabilistic models involves a dimensionality reduction technique in generative adversarial networks, allowing the model to generate samples from a lower dimensional space that approximates the real data distribution. However, this method suffers from several limitations, including the difficulty in switching between different conditions in a piecewise manner, the inability to use external knowledge, and the tendency to produce samples that are far removed from the real data distribution. To address these issues, a novel method has been proposed that uses a lower dimensional space to represent conditioning variables, rather than the original space. By doing so, the model can learn a more organized manifold in the latent space that captures the underlying patterns in the conditioning variables, and switch between conditions in a seamless and gradual manner. Additionally, external knowledge can be incorporated into the model by aligning the latent space with the underlying structure of the conditioning variables. Experimental results have shown that this method outperforms existing techniques in terms of sample quality and conditioning accuracy, and produces more natural and continuous transitions between conditions.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling technique must be utilized, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Researchers have developed various methods to create these samples, such as methods like slice sampling and its derivatives. A study examined multiple variants of slice sampling and a log-likelihood transformation technique called the complex transformation, as well as its connection to a method called the complex slice sampler. To compare these methods, nested sampling tasks were conducted on a set of complex astronomical and astrophysical models, and the performance of each method was evaluated based on efficiency and accuracy. Results showed that the complex transformation and complex slice sampler achieve significantly higher efficiency compared to traditional nested sampling techniques, while preserving accurate results.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distance between any two of them, excluding the third. Our work proves that we can create a brief description for each point in a plane with a small increase in its complexity, allowing it to tolerate some missing distance queries. More specifically, we can create a description that uses $O(\log^3 n)$ bits per point with the ability to handle $\Omega(\log n)$ faults while still determining the direct distance in the presence of faults. Using this framework, we can also design a system for distributing messages in plane networks that requires minimal redundancy and can function even if some messages are lost.

In this study, we investigate two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation. Our mean-field solution accurately predicts a discrete mode emerging from the dissipation-driven many-body ground state, and this mode exhibits characteristics of a parametric amplifier under specific conditions. By analyzing the correlation function at short times, we find that two-particle correlations follow the pattern expected of three distinct states, with a meta-stable state intervening on the way to equilibration. Furthermore, our analysis in the frequency domain reveals that, in accordance with established theories, the correlation function exhibits non-analytical behavior at two specific points, with a gap developing at one point and negative frequencies emerging at the other.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, satisfying certain smoothness conditions and $\lambda \in L^2(\Omega)$, we demonstrate the existence of a weak solution in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ for $p > 2$, under the condition that the equation is supplemented with homogeneous boundary conditions.

Recent advancements in machine learning have led to the development of robust
Gaussian Process (GP) layers that can learn from data efficiently. These GP
layers have been successfully applied to various self-supervised learning tasks,
enabling them to identify reliable assumptions in data patterns. However, GP
layers from unsupervised learning may not effectively detect out-of-distribution
data, particularly when encountering noisy labels from supervised learning.
Therefore, it is crucial to establish a benchmark to evaluate their performance in
out-of-distribution detection. To address this challenge, we propose a new GP layer
that utilizes distributional information to distinguish in- and out-of-distribution
inputs. Our approach is validated through experiments on various self-supervised
and semi-supervised learning tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in
out-of-distribution detection.

In systems that are driven far from equilibrium, unusual phenomena can occur, and our study demonstrates one such example: the emergence of a condensate in an otherwise non-stationary state of an open optical lattice that is excited by a two-photon laser. The interplay between heat generated by the driving and the lattice's non-closed boundaries leads to an increase in a specific energy level, and eventually, a Bose-Einstein condensate forms in this level. We found that this condensate shares similarities with a'scar' - a set of eigenstates that retain a connection to the initial quantum state, and our proposed experiment aims to observe this condensate and the'scar' in an optical lattice that is not in a state of equilibrium.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain with a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side, along with specific boundary data. A key finding demonstrates that a strengthened version of the Alexandrov maximum principle can be applied to the convex solution. Furthermore, under certain boundary conditions, it has been proven that the convex solution exhibits uniform H\"older continuity. A key component in proving these results involves the application of a recently discovered estimate for the first derivative of the convex solution, which plays a crucial role.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant challenge. We've now made progress in constructing optical clocks that can accurately measure time. Although these devices don't need human intervention once they're set in motion, their operation often relies on previous knowledge of how to modulate the laser used in its construction. We've found a way to characterize optical clocks by analyzing statistical patterns in events that don't recur regularly. By doing so, we can measure the passage of time without relying on traditional timekeeping methods. Using an algorithm, we can reconstruct a reliable time scale from data collected over an extended period. We've tested this approach by collecting data from a Dicke clock, which uses rubidium vapor and Dicke-laser light, under two different conditions. We've compared our results to data collected using a more conventional method that relies on periodic patterns. Our technique is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of optical clocks, which will facilitate development and testing.

This research proposes an efficient network management framework that leverages a fog environment to ensure high-quality service delivery. The framework focuses on managing service delivery, network resources, and service processing nodes to achieve optimal performance. To achieve this goal, the framework implements real-time service scheduling, network configuration, and service failure mitigation through adaptive fog node selection, dynamic service scaling, and proactive fault prevention. The framework also includes an energy-efficient strategy to minimize the service delivery delay and reduce energy consumption. Performance results show that the framework effectively implements real-time service scheduling, network configuration, fault prevention, and energy-efficient management. Compared to other methods, the framework achieves lower service delivery delays and reduced energy consumption while ensuring on-time service delivery.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in different classes. Various pair-wise loss techniques can be understood by'surgery' which involves setting specific gradient directions. We categorize six pair-wise loss techniques into three groups based on two criteria - the direction of the gradient and whether images in different classes are used as negative samples. Our findings show that only one of the technique, which includes negative samples from the same class, can improve compactness of the embedding. This enables the model to recognize images of the same class as distinct, even if they look different. Additionally, our analysis reveals that using negative samples from different classes causes the model to mark images of the same class as negative, resulting in the model failing to recognize images of the same class as distinct. Our analysis also shows that the performance of the model can be improved by combining different pair-wise loss techniques.

In this context, we explore a specific type of quantum error-correcting codes derived from conformal pyramids of holographic nets, which serve as models for white-box Reisner diagrams. A particular subclass of these codes, hyper-invariant MERAs, possess enhanced characteristics, ensuring their quantum and classical versions have enhanced resilience. Importantly, their quantum error-correcting capabilities are limited only to the specific type of errors originating from non-trivial, isotropic states, while their classical error-correcting capabilities are restricted to specific types of bit-flips and phase-flips. A key aspect of hyper-invariant MERAs is that their quantum and classical error-correcting capabilities can be seamlessly integrated into a unified, anisotropic state, which is only possible due to their unique white-box Reisner diagram structure. This integrated anisotropic state exhibits distinct, power-law-like correlations, which are unique to hyper-invariant MERAs and distinguish them from standard invariant MERAs. A key outcome of this integration is that it allows hyper-invariant MERAs to achieve an enhanced thermodynamic limit compared to standard invariant MERAs, which is only possible due to their hyper-invariant property.

Filaments in molecular clouds form elongated structures due to factors like magnetic fields and dynamic instability. These magnetic fields can influence the formation of filaments, including their shape and size. The proximity of filaments to neighboring structures is affected by factors like magnetic fields and heat, and can be studied to determine the prevalence of magnetic field dominance. By examining a 20x10 parsec region around the Galactic Center containing 1032 filaments, researchers found that 80% of these filaments have a nearby counterpart within a 5.5 parsec radius. The distribution of distances to neighboring filaments shows a peak at 5.5 parsec, and is relatively uniform in right ascension and declination. The density of these nearby filaments is constant at approximately 0.3 parsec/steradian, and is unaffected by a filament's proximity to the Galactic Center. The separation between these filaments follows a power-law distribution, and is primarily composed of smaller separations (<5.5 parsec). The average density of these nearby filaments is constant, and is not influenced by a filament's size or proximity to the Galactic Center. The average magnetic energy in these filaments is significantly higher than the thermal energy, and is sufficient to explain their alignment. These findings support the hypothesis that these filaments are influenced by magnetic fields, and are not primarily composed of magnetically-induced structures.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs through the scheduling of smart inverters. The method considers primary-secondary networks and loads influenced by voltage. The system complexity is reduced through the introduction of an alternating voltage-dependent power model and the use of ADMM for combining distributed strategies for DERs and the secondary system. The method uses a leader-follower approach to demonstrate its ability to reach optimal CVR levels at the distribution level, while also considering constraints at the grid edge. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical tests on a 118-bus distribution system, showing that it can reduce energy losses and lower peak demand without compromising stability.

In traditional bandit and expert problems, decision-making processes incur uniform costs across all time. This paper deviates from that convention by considering scenarios where delays between actions vary in relation to the chosen arms. It presents a class of problems with inherent structural connections and develops both upper and lower bounds for algorithms operating within this framework under a new performance metric. Furthermore, the results are applied to a real-world task, i.e., optimizing ad display durations for maximum user satisfaction. To address this problem, a novel learning algorithm is designed, which demonstrates optimal performance when measured by a metric representing user satisfaction.

Current text generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed, producing responses that lack naturalness, coherence, and relevance. To improve upon these limitations, this paper outlines a new framework, LEATHER, designed to facilitate research in generating text that mimics human communication. The framework comprises three key areas of focus: a set of learning objectives grounded in established theories of verbal human interaction; a flexible representation format for processing utterances as relationships between words and meanings; and a recommended approach for developing a flexible model architecture that can learn to produce coherent, context-specific text through incremental updates and fine-tuning.

Following World War II, researchers in the field of quantum chromodynamics were presented with an initial challenge: determining the temperature at which nuclear matter transitions into a quark-gluon plasma, a state of the art theoretical model. Given the function's complexity and non-perturbative nature, this task proved insurmountable for decades. The development of Monte Carlo methods marked a significant turning point, although the methods were initially confined to small lattices due to computational constraints. As technology advanced, it became possible to design and analyze larger, more complex simulations, pushing the boundaries of what could be achieved. The resulting advancements have led to breakthroughs in understanding the properties of this unknown state, the quark-gluon plasma, providing a foundation for future studies of the early universe and high-energy collisions between heavy ions.

We utilize probabilistic machine learning to predict the uncertainty in loads experienced by offshore wind turbines under various atmospheric conditions. By combining data from meteorological models with load measurements from turbines, we develop a predictive model that accounts for the uncertainty in loads resulting from different weather patterns. This involves using Gaussian Process regression in a sequential manner to successively refine our predictions based on weather parameters such as wind speed, wind direction, and sea state. Our improved method is evaluated against traditional load prediction techniques and turbulence models, demonstrating superior performance when tested on real-world data from two offshore wind farms.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective early warning systems. In this study, we examine the feasibility of using Twitter data to predict the magnitude of earthquakes by examining user reactions prior to an earthquake in Izmir, a city in Turkey. Our analysis leverages 1,523,371 tweets collected from the 30th of September 2021 to the 6th of February 2022, including the devastating M7.0 Izmir earthquake that occurred on October 30, 2021. Our findings show that Izmir residents began expressing distress on Twitter approximately 28 minutes before the earthquake, with user anxiety surpassing objectivity. An anomaly detection model applied to tweet data identified instances of natural disasters, revealing that the annotations provided by human evaluators align with the detected anomalies. Our research demonstrates that the patterns in NLP representations of tweets can forecast the magnitude of earthquakes by utilizing logistic regression models.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such a case, we determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for nilpotent quotients $G//\Gamma$ to possess property $R_\infty$, given that $\Gamma$ is a generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultrafast experiments and is based on optimizing a trajectory description with respect to experimental measurements. Application of the variational principle with a Lagrangian that includes only experimental data yields equations that expand and simplify to a set of ordinary differential equations describing how trajectories change over time. To solve these equations effectively, a minimal set of initial conditions is determined by minimizing the difference between the equations and the available experimental data. As demonstrated by simulations and real-world experiments, incorporating trajectory changes can significantly improve the outcome of data processing, especially when the underlying dynamics are complex and subject to uncertainties.

We introduce SceNDD, a unique dataset consisting of 20,596 scenarios derived from the NDD dataset, which was obtained through naturalistic driving observations. Utilizing our previously validated method based on task-driven object detection and scenario generation, the scenarios in SceNDD accurately capture real-world situations encountered by drivers. In contrast to synthetic datasets, the scenarios in SceNDD are free from the limitations of simulated environments. While naturalistic datasets offer authentic data, they are restricted by the diversity of scenarios encountered during collection. To mitigate this, we employed NDD, an extended naturalistic driving dataset, and extracted diverse scenarios from it. Our novel approach then assigned scenario labels and inter-relational metadata to SceNDD. To evaluate SceNDD's potential, we conducted two experiments: scenario detection and scenario-based detection tasks. The results demonstrate SceNDD's distinct value in object detection and scenario-based applications.

In connection with the reflected entropy proposal $F_R(X,Y)=-\log Z_X(Y)$, we explored the relationship between state renewal and conformal field theory. We discovered a reflected entropy formula for a pair of adjacent conformal interfaces. This formula was then applied to various boundary and interface entanglement entropy calculations. We verified that it accurately reproduces mirror dual entanglement entropy in holographic contexts. We also derived a first-order boundary entropy Yang-Mills field theory.

Research into Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has been gaining momentum due to RIS's ability to direct incoming signals and amplify specific channels while minimizing weak channels. However, accurate channel estimation is crucial for initial RIS settings and has become a pressing issue. This study addresses the challenge of channel estimation in OFDM systems assisted by RIS that utilize a limited cyclic prefix and deal with hardware imperfections. A deep neural network enhanced by an early stopping mechanism is introduced to replace traditional pilot-based channel estimation. Our results show that the proposed solution achieves a satisfactory performance within 98% of the conventional method's accuracy with only 50% of the traditional pilot-based channel estimation. Furthermore, the model's adaptability is demonstrated across various scenarios, including changes in the number of training epochs, training samples, feature dimensionality, and hardware imperfections.

We have discovered a single system observing the fluctuation dynamics of a measurable quantity using non-projective measurement processes. Our research indicates that, at the single system level, the integral fluctuation theorem is only upheld when accounting for positive fluctuations and not negative ones. Notably, the mean energy fluctuation in a closed system observed through projective measurement processes satisfies the integral fluctuation theorem. However, we demonstrate that, at the level of the system observer, the mean energy fluctuation does not adhere to the integral fluctuation theorem when either maximum or minimum energy measurements occur.

We are investigating the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of dimension 8.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has led to widespread social isolation, economic difficulties, and a significant death toll, prompting the development of contact tracing technology to mitigate its spread.  As a result, contact tracing technology has become a critical tool for controlling the pandemic, with an increasing number of national contact tracing systems being developed to combat the disease.  These systems, which are designed to promote user cooperation, have the potential to save lives by helping track the spread of the virus.  However, they also pose significant risks to users' personal data, which can be compromised in a global setting where multiple jurisdictions are involved.  In this study, we examine the privacy risks associated with national contact tracing systems, specifically focusing on Brazil's Coronav\'irus-SUS application, which is one of the first systems to be implemented on a national scale.  Our analysis reveals a significant vulnerability in the Coronav\'irus-SUS app, which could potentially compromise users' sensitive information, prompting the development of a more secure architecture to safeguard user data and protect national contact tracing systems from unauthorized access.

We present a comprehensive overview of quantum information principles and
apply them to neural structures in an organic framework. Quantum coherence and
entanglement are examined in the context of neuronal and brain function,
wherever possible, utilizing language-free quantum information principles for
clarity. Relevant quantum information theory is covered, supplemented by a
mathematical review of the underlying Hilbert space formalism, to provide a
self-contained explanation, even for those without prior knowledge of the
subject. The document is divided into three parts, the first focusing on the
application of quantum information principles to systems such as single neurons,
synapses, and glial cells, the second examining collective quantum effects in
neural systems, and the third discussing open systems and the dynamics of
neural quantum behavior within the context of Markov evolution. An appendix is
added to clarify the mathematical notation employed throughout the
documentary, where relevant Hilbert space formalism is reviewed, along with
the most relevant open systems and Markov evolution.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young asteroid families discovered recently on the planetoid Ceres, specifically locations $(2.77,1.84,1.65)^\circ$ and $(3.23,1.84,1.65)^\circ$ in ecliptic coordinates, has been examined. It involves a situation where an outer member $(39991)$ Iochroma perturbs an inner member $(383584)$ Ichinozaki. This interaction triggers a specific resonance $3:1$ between their orbital periods. In the future, another object may take the place of Ichinozoka as the inner member of the family, but for now, Iochroma is the dominant factor in shaping the family's structure. A detailed analysis has been conducted to confirm the family's composition and the role of Iochroma's perturbations in shaping Ichinozaki's orbit. This analysis has been compared to previous studies and confirmed their accuracy. It has also been found that Iochroma's perturbations affect not just Ichinozaki, the central object,  but also other outer objects, including $(383585)$ Ichinozakib. This is due to a complex chain reaction of gravitational pull. A plot has been provided to visualize the timing of Iochroma's perturbations affecting Ichinozaki's orbit over the past few thousand years.

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression using the Hurwitz zeta function. We introduce a novel integral kernel that relates to the Hurwitz zeta function and serves as an extension of the integral kernel linked to the Ramanujan identity. Furthermore, we derive additional results, including a generalization of the binary Bernoulli polynomial and we offer a simplified proof of one of Ramanujan's identities for odd zeta values.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition feature. Specifically, we show that these theories decompose into a product of T-equivariant rational cohomology and a two-fold T^2-equivariant rational cohomology. This key decomposition enables us to leverage the findings from Nekovár and Geller for T and T^2 equivariant cohomology respectively, to obtain the T equivariant cohomology of complex projective spaces.

In recent years, industry and the scientific community have converged on using machine learning extensively. From image recognition to drug design and plate tectonics analysis to astrobiology, machine learning has far-reaching applications. The field of algebraic geometry, however, has yet to fully embrace machine learning, mainly due to concerns over integrating it into existing mathematical frameworks. The following discussion will explore the benefits of incorporating machine learning into algebraic geometry, featuring a new method for generating classification charts through machine learning. This method employs a trained CNN, modeled after state-of-the-art computer games, to identify and classify geometric shapes, particularly essential for studying complex phenomena in cosmology and theoretical high-energy physics.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of $J/\psi$ angular distributions in $pp \to J/\psi + \eta_c(\chi_{cJ}) + X \to J/\psi + \eta_c(\chi_{cJ}) \mu^+ \mu^- + X \to J/\psi + \eta_c(\chi_{cJ}) \gamma^* \gamma^+ \mu^- \mu^+ + X$ processes at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV. We utilize data from Belle, in addition to proposed, experiments, to investigate the phenomenon. We evaluate the distortion of predicted distributions by the $J/\psi$ spin alignment, in both transverse and longitudinal states, as well as the effects of $\eta_c$ and $\chi_{cJ}$ spin alignment, to analyze the distortion factor, $\mathcal{A}$, and compare it with the $\sin^2 \theta_t$ factor, to discuss its implications for $J/\psi$ polarization measurements.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of Signal for all users, improving product education and functionality is essential to enhance the security mindset of casual users and boost overall user security.

This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of products involving the solar irradiance function, as defined by ASTM standards, and user-defined smooth functions. The method's ability to produce accurate results with minimal evaluations is particularly beneficial due to the non-uniform nature of the solar irradiance, which cannot be adequately approximated by a polynomial of a low degree. The accompanying Julia code facilitates the computation of solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rules for any required precision, allowing users to specify the number of points needed in addition to the integration limits, solar panel height, and Earth-equivalent radius.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation holds significant value in developing training algorithms for deep networks. However, current methods based on automatic differentiation and Kronecker-factored block diagonal approximations fall short of achieving optimal performance. This paper presents the ViViT structure, a new way to compute curvatures that yields the generalized Gauss-Newton approximation with minimal computational and memory costs. This is achieved by leveraging ViViT structures from submanifolds of linear maps. By implementing the technique, researchers can develop faster first-order optimization methods and improve explanation and interpretation of model behavior. Experimental results show that ViViT-based methods can achieve a 50 times speedup over existing approaches, like PyTorch-CG, for Hessian-vector products.

Numerous languages attribute gender not only to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. For instance, consider a French text describing a gender-neutral car using the masculine form "il" instead of "le". In order to improve the accuracy of neural language models for inanimate objects with a focus on their physical properties, we must address how grammatical gender influences how these objects are perceived. We investigated this by collecting 1000 sentences from Wikipedia articles about cars and evaluating how grammatical gender affects how these nouns are represented semantically, particularly in terms of their attributes. We discovered that changing a car's grammatical gender from masculine to feminine would lead to a significant shift in its associated attributes, with approximately 60% of those attributes changing. Notably, this effect is more pronounced in cars than other inanimate objects, such as parts or brands.

We establish that if a non-archimedean local group is semi-simple and unipotent, then it meets specific criteria under certain conditions, affecting its 1-cohomology values and the structure of its center. This condition is characterized by a specific relationship between the dimensions of irreducible characters and the group's algebraic dimension. Furthermore, this result has implications for arithmetic groups and their algebraic properties. Specifically, under certain Gelfand-Petrov conditions, we demonstrate that groups like surface quaternion groups are "stiff" and do not exhibit a specific, earlier described phenomenon known as "charm". This result has further implications for the classification of groups with 1-cohomology values.

Estimating an object's pose is a critical problem in many fields. Current approaches are limited by their reliance on extensive data for specific objects and categories. In contrast, we propose a novel method that can infer poses for objects without prior knowledge of the object categories involved. Our approach leverages a few example images for each object of interest and relies on a rotational 2D pose detector and a novel inverse rendering technique to determine 3D pose. Our results indicate that this method can effectively use fewer object images to achieve accurate results, and that incorporating more images will simply enhance our approach's accuracy. This is a significant advancement over existing object-based pose estimation techniques. Our approach demonstrates this advantage on a range of challenging datasets, including category-level poses across multiple objects.

Predicting short-term traffic is a complex problem, particularly with short notice periods and limited data availability. Existing forecasting models often struggle due to the sparsity and short-term nature of the data. In this paper, a new approach is proposed by transforming the forecasting task into a regression problem using extracted features from sequential traffic patterns. An encoder-decoder model architecture is developed, incorporating temporal attention to prioritize pattern sequences, sequential features to account for interdependent data, and hierarchical features to capture both short-term and long-term patterns, as well as a hidden feature extractor using similarity measures to capture the complexities of sparse traffic systems. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of this new approach over traditional methods, and that it can be further improved by incorporating additional spatial information.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders designed to handle interventions and counterfactual scenarios. VACA includes two key models: a variational Gaussian Bayesian Network Model (GBN-VCA) that captures the underlying structure of networks given observational data and interventions, and a variational Counterfactual Bayesian Network Model (CBN-VCA) built upon GBN-VCA that allows for the simulation of unobserved network connections and counterfactual scenarios. By using stochastic variational inference, our models automatically find the best variational approximations for interventions and counterfactual scenarios. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our models through numerical simulations and real-world applications, such as predicting voter behavior based on social network data.

The Radio Observations of LOFAR at Jansky (ROLEJ) program utilizes the Irish LOFAR station to carry out continuous and real-time surveillance above 200 MHz with a high sensitivity to broad-band signals. Recent studies demonstrated the station's ability to detect the outbursts of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) and Gigahertz Peaked Spectrum (GPS) sources. The Irish LOFAR station is equipped with the REAL-time Transient Acquisition backend (REALTA), an innovative system capable of storing and processing LoFAR data in real-time. REALTA enables the system to identify various types of transients such as FRBs, GPS sources, and other solar transients within the stored data. In this study, REALTA was used to analyze LoFAR data over a period of 153 days and compared its performance with existing transient surveys. The results indicate that REALTA was able to identify known FRBs and GPS sources, achieving a detection rate comparable to other surveys such as the NANOGrav FRB Catalogue and the GLEAM survey. The results of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of REALTA in enabling the ongoing search for FRBs and GPS sources at the Irish LOFAR station.

In an era where big data analytics driven by machine learning is revolutionizing
our daily lives, we believe that traditional methods of photonics will greatly
benefit from integration with machine learning. This integration, known as
metaphotonics, involves the interference of multiple light waves to produce a
predictable outcome. By leveraging the inherent parallelism in photonic systems,
metaphotonics can offer a level of performance superiority unattainable with
electronic systems. However, developing metaphotonics is a complex task that
requires precise control over complex light patterns. To overcome this challenge,
we propose a novel approach that combines machine learning with metaphotonics to
automatically design, analyze, and optimize the system's performance. This
breakthrough enables the creation of highly advanced optical systems, including
high-speed data transfer and ultra-sensitive sensors, using a single laser and
deflecting light with nanostructures. Using cutting-edge techniques such as
deep learning and data transfer simulations, we have successfully designed and
engineered a fully functional data transfer system and ultra-sensitive optical
sensor, paving the way for machine learning-driven metaphotonics and the
development of next-generation optical systems.

The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office is crucial. In this research, a dataset containing 3,514 movies from 1990 to 2019 was created to study this phenomenon. By examining the relationships between movie attributes such as budget, runtime, and cast size, and its overall revenue, a model was developed to forecast the gross revenue of upcoming movies. Surprisingly, research found that movie attributes like budget, runtime, and number of actors actually decrease the predicted revenue, while factors like movie genre, release date, and production studio have a positive impact. This counterintuitive result may be due to attributes like budget and runtime influencing revenue through other factors, such as movie quality and marketing efforts.

The energy shift poses a threat to the stability of the power grid's operation, 
which necessitates maintaining both voltage amplitude and frequency within 
safe limits. Research has primarily concentrated on the stability and 
frequency dynamics but largely overlooked voltage stability. This work aims to 
investigate the stability of simple networks through both linear analysis and 
nonlinear examination, specifically focusing on how energy storage with 
battery capacity affects it. We will also explore and evaluate strategies 
for secondary frequency control that consider both frequency and voltage 
stability.

Cyber Physical Systems are transforming into cohesive units known as Systems of Systems by integrating with other CPSs, forming complex metropolitan areas that enhance quality of life for human residents. A notable example is the development of smart infrastructure systems that support human well-being, exemplified by air quality monitoring networks and traffic management systems. As these Systems of Systems continue to evolve, they will address pressing issues such as climate change, encompassing urban planning, transportation, and energy systems. However, achieving this goal requires significant challenges be overcome, including the integration of diverse and often competing systems, each with unique objectives and operational methods, into a unified, cooperative unit. A System of Systems is defined as an entity consisting of independent subsystems working together to achieve common goals, but achieving this requires substantial technical obstacles be overcome, including the integration of diverse and often competing systems, into a unified, cohesive unit. A key requirement for achieving this goal is the development of intelligent Systems of Systems, equipped with autonomous decision-making capabilities, facilitated by Machine Intelligence. This paper outlines a comprehensive approach to empowering CPS and SoS with Machine Intelligence, utilizing a dual-layered knowledge representation of goals and physical reality, translated into a graph for machine processing. This format enables the application of advanced Machine Intelligence algorithms, initially developed for autonomous vehicle navigation, to guide SoS decision-making and goal achievement. This approach is demonstrated through two case studies, one involving the collaboration of two disparate urban transportation systems, and another with two energy and heating infrastructure systems, showcasing

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions, researchers can gain insights into the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets. This study employs a Monte-Carlo code, partially polarized inverse Compton scattering in MAPPIES, to model polarized and non-polarized Compton backscattering in blazars exhibiting UV/soft X-ray excess. Our findings suggest that a combination of non-polarized and polarized Compton scattering can effectively reproduce the observed polarization patterns in the PKS 2151-003 system, which is characterized by intense polarization in the X-ray band and variable polarization in the UV band.

In the context of random matrix theory and its application to complex analytic continuation, we investigate the general pattern according to which eigenvalues continue analytically across singularities in the complex plane. This eigenvalue pattern serves as a model for the yet unresolved puzzle of analytically continuing partition functions over complex landscapes. Although we do not fully resolve this issue here, our results provide essential insights that significantly narrow the gap between the model and the actual problem. Our findings can be extended to other areas, such as the representation of characteristic polynomials and the application of gauge theories solving heavy quark problems.

To develop optimal strategies for real-time analysis of quantum systems, it's necessary to create effective methods for recognizing specific states in an ongoing process. This work focuses on designing an algorithm that enables the identification of pure symmetric states in higher-dimensional systems through repeated measurements, enabling the determination of specific states with a level of certainty that grows as least as well as the maximum probability of the most difficult, analogous states. This research further extends existing non-real-time methods by providing a clear protocol that can be executed in the laboratory for the proper state to be identified.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized model of QCD strings that fragment and contribute to particle formation. Baryons are formed when QCD strings quantized and break apart, resulting in the emission of Lattice gluons. These gluons condense into quark-antiquark pairs and lattice instantons. When helical QCD strings fragment, the resulting lattice gluons form quark-quark triads, resulting in the creation of baryons.

In the helioseismic technique used to study the solar interior, the speed of sound is calculated by analyzing the travel times of waves emitted by active regions. A key factor in this method is the movement of plasma around active regions, which affects the speed of sound measurements by altering north-south helioseismic diagrams. An analysis of the Solar Dynamics Observatory's images revealed that these plasma flows play a crucial role in active regions. An idealized model was developed to simulate the effect of these plasma flows in different configurations, and it showed that they impact travel-time measurements by up to 10 seconds. This effect was found to be highly dependent on the orientation of the active region's magnetic field and its shape. A mathematical formula was also derived to estimate the impact of these plasma flows on helioseismic travel-time measurements, and it was applied to real active regions to quantify their effect. The results showed that using spherical harmonics to describe the shape of active regions provides an accurate basis for modeling the associated plasma flows.

Researchers have proposed a theory suggesting that cosmic strings could have generated the large-scale magnetic fields seen in the universe. These magnetic fields, if they existed, would have produced gravitational waves that can be detected by the Pulsar Timing Array, potentially revealing information about their formation. A new study explores this correlation, using data on the scales and energy densities of these gravitational waves to determine the properties of the primordial magnetic fields. A minimum scale of $10^{-6}$ has been established for the cosmic string network, with the possibility of finer details depending on the details of the magnetic fields' evolution.

Light field technology is a highly regarded candidate for the next generation of image representation and 3D display. Despite its capabilities, existing approaches face challenges in efficiently encoding and compressing light field data for practical applications. Traditional methods often rely on models that treat all disparity levels equally, leading to suboptimal performance. In contrast, our proposed approach leverages the insights of a pre-trained disparity model to develop disparity-aware neural network components for each level of disparity, resulting in more effective compression. This strategy is applied to the core components of a light field representation, including the 4D sub-aperture image domain. By adopting a two-stage learning process and utilizing a disparity-agnostic convolutional neural network, our approach achieves superior performance in light field image compression, as evidenced by our results on the LF-COMP dataset, where our method surpasses 100 benchmarks in terms of PSNR-SSIM metric.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two primary models, interactive and non-interactive, employ different approaches to learn a common representation space for different languages.  While interactive models like the MMAP algorithm yield better results, non-interactive models such as the ITOM algorithm are preferred due to their simplicity and the ability to precompute queries without needing source data. This paper investigates the performance of non-interactive and interactive models for cross-lingual information retrieval and proposes a new hybrid approach that leverages the strengths of both. By merging ITOM and MMAP, we demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing methods and shows promising potential for improvement.

Developing reliable models for forecasting health metrics in low and middle-income countries is an intricate task, largely due to the absence of detailed, detailed data, and the need to generate small-area estimates based on national averages. In this scenario, combining design-based and model-based statistical methods may offer an effective solution. A recent study examined the application of this approach to estimating under-five and maternal mortality rates in Kenya using the 2008-2009 DHS survey. A discrete area-based strategy was employed, with results indicating that this combination of methods yields accurate estimates at both the national and provincial levels, and outperforms models relying solely on linear or quadratic spatial predictors. A potential drawback of this approach is the lack of uncertainty quantification, and the reliance on a design-based survey. To mitigate this, a second study adapted the area-based strategy to model-based estimation, using a hypothetical synthetic population. Results showed that this modified method yields accurate estimates, and is less dependent on the accuracy of the synthetic population. A major advantage of this approach is the ability to quantify uncertainty.

We explore the application of quantum theory to modeling casino operations, focusing on a scenario where betting outcomes are based on continuous variables like money. Our analysis, grounded in the principles of quantum theory, reveals that casinos can be viewed as having a superior advantage. We achieve this by comparing betting strategies, referred to as policies, that either utilize or disregard quantum principles. Our results indicate that as the scale of the casino increases, policies that adhere to quantum principles tend to yield progressively lower returns. We further demonstrate that optimal policies can be distinguished by certain key characteristics, which serve as distinct signatures, or features, distinctive to the casino's advantage.

Using ab initio calculations, we investigate two-dimensional semiconducting materials with a specific crystal structure, identified as MGe$_2$N$_4$ where M can be Mo, W, or Ti and Ge can be Si or Ge. We employ a supercell approach to analyze and discuss the one-dimensional density of states, quasiparticle band structure, and stacking-dependent electronic properties. Furthermore, we examine the influence of different types of neighboring atoms on the band alignment and identify type-II band alignments in MoSi$_2$N$_6$ and WSi$_2$N$_6$. Additionally, we analyze the influence of different types of neighboring atoms on the band alignment in their heterostructures, suggesting that these materials have potential as thermoelectric materials due to their unique band alignments. We also investigate the influence of external stimuli, such as uniaxial strain and transverse electric fields, on the band structure and band gaps. We discover that these external stimuli result in large changes to the band gaps, indicating that these materials have potential as nonvolatile memory devices.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra.

The magnetic field and non-ideal factors are known to influence the collapse of a prestellar core, ultimately restricting the formation of the protostar and triggering the development of a rotating, flared disk. Research into core collapse dynamics, including magnetic field effects, has been extensively reviewed, with a focus on the resulting disk structure and angular momentum transport mechanisms. These studies indicate that disk accretion onto the protostar is necessary for the protostar to reach the mass required for the operation of radiative feedback, with variations in magnetic field and non-ideal factors affecting disk accretion. Furthermore, disk accretion enables the development of a flared and spiraling structure, with examples of such disks observed in arches and in the B335 system. Angular momentum transport in disks is thought to result from non-axisymmetric instabilities, with one theory supported by core collapse simulations and another by observations of non-axisymmetric structures in protostellar disks.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by the Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies with wavelength. Observations made under low atmospheric conditions, such as during sunrise or sunset, provide valuable data for creating atmospheric models. By analyzing on-site data from a 1.65 m telescope located at La Silla in Chile, a dataset of over 700 atmospheric models was developed. Each model consists of 16 coefficients that describe the atmospheric dispersion's dependence on wavelength and atmospheric conditions. By analyzing the distribution of these coefficients, a mean atmosphere was established, and a method to determine the uncertainty of the models was established, showing a 10% margin of error for coefficients 3 and 4. Furthermore, a study of the variability of the models across different solar zenith angles revealed a 10% change for the first four coefficients and a 5% change for the remaining coefficients, suggesting that the models can be applied to a range of solar zenith angles.

This paper presents a state-space model for multi-period time series data that
utilizes an non-parametric distribution to capture the patterns and correlations
between each time period's factors. We apply a Bayesian approach using Bayesian
Gaussian Process, and combine it with a time series model that uses a non-parametric
distribution, resulting in a model that can identify relationships between time
periods and components. Our proposed model effectively handles sparse data and
complex dependencies between time series, and is suitable for multiple sequence
data. Simulation studies and a real-world stock analysis demonstrate the model's
capacity for predictive and analytical purposes.

In a setting that combines continuous logic, we establish a connection between Stone duality and Pontryagin duality by treating Pontryagin duality as a particular instance of Stone duality. This is achieved in the context of a topological abelian group $A$, and its associated group $\mathcal{F}(A)$ of continuous automorphisms. Utilizing the continuous logic framework, we show that the structure of $\mathcal{F}(A)$ can be effectively described using a first-order formula, and that this duality extends to the spectrum of compact abelian groups. This extended duality reveals a novel connection between the theory of continuous logic and Pontryagin duality.

The rapid growth in the number of devices allows for a vast amount of data to be collected, whether in private settings, as part of a public duty, or to maintain individual anonymity. Due to the sensitive nature of this data, it often can't be shared openly for the models to be trained. A solution to this challenge has been developed, known as Federated Learning, which allows a central server to train models using client data without direct access to it. Despite providing data privacy through differential privacy and trying to be fair in training models, ensuring both is challenging. In this paper, we explore the complexities of simultaneously achieving fairness, data privacy, and model accuracy in Federated Learning systems. Specifically, we examine the trade-offs between utilizing differential privacy and fairness in FL, including the impact of DPD on fairness and model accuracy, and how fairness and model accuracy are affected by DPD.

We present a supersymmetric extension of the $U(1)_X$ model, featuring a new gauge symmetry, together with right-handed neutrinos, which can serve as dark matter candidates. Following discovery at the LHC, we focus on the underlying $R$-parity, which likely gives rise to a sign of $\sigma(pp\to \tilde f^\pm \tilde f^\mp)$ in the absence of edge events in $\sigma(pp\to \tilde f^0 \tilde f^0)$. Our model offers an explanation for the dark matter density, neutrino masses, and baryon number asymmetry, likely giving rise to a long-lived, neutralino dark matter candidate, which could be discovered at the LHC or explained by FRB observations.

We investigate a smart reflecting surface-aided wireless-powered communication network where a multi-antenna energy transmitter broadcasts an exclusive energy signal to a powered transmitter that then broadcasts an information signal to the destination despite interference from multiple concurrent energy links. To optimize this system, we developed a novel, highly efficient deep learning design that uses unsupervised methods to find the optimal reflecting parameters for maximum system throughput. A key component of our design is the creation of a training dataset that abstracts out the underlying system dynamics, enabling an unsupervised deep learning approach. We demonstrate that our proposed method approximates optimal performance and outperforms a comparable, but less efficient, model-based design.

For the first time, researchers used total absorption gamma spectroscopy to measure the Gamow-Teller strength distribution in $^{186}$Hg decaying into $^{186}$Au and compared it to theoretical QRPA calculations employing the SLy4 Skyrme force. The measured strength distribution, alongside the nuclei's half-lives, is best explained by incorporating a combination of prolate and oblate configurations independently in the parent and daughter nuclei. Prolate components dominated both parent and daughter nuclei for the measured strength distribution, indicating the necessity of incorporating prolate configurations to describe the beta decay process. The calculated and measured strengths aligned closely for the beta feeders, but the beta feedings were lower than expected for the beta decayers. The calculated and measured energies of the low-lying states matched well with each other. The calculated half-life for $^{186}$Hg was approximately 18.9 seconds, comparable to the measured half-life of 18.7 seconds.

We explore the intersection of dark matter and leptogenesis within a unified theoretical framework, which includes three right-handed neutrinos, a fermionic dark matter particle, and two additional scalar fields beyond the Standard Model. The interaction between these scalar fields influences both the dark matter and leptonic sectors. Dark matter stability is ensured by a combination of protection mechanisms, while the connection between the two scalar fields and right-handed neutrinos enables both dark matter and leptogenesis to occur naturally. By doing so, we examine the relationship between the two processes and demonstrate that their connection can lead to significant increases in both dark matter and neutrino masses.

We've developed an algorithm that can learn to control a system just by observing one trial of data collection, using past experience and offline data. This approach works by leveraging correlations between various pieces of information: one system's behavior, its reward function, and offline data of similar systems' behaviors and reward functions. In order to make data collection more efficient, we've formulated an offline data selection method that identifies the most informative systems' behaviors ahead of time, and our results are supported by theoretical analysis and demonstrated in several experiments including a quadrotor flight simulator.

This paper derives and analyzes the Toda Toda-identity in the context of conformal field theory for Toda, specifically for the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model. We establish a comprehensive set of Toda-identities that encompass the stress tensor, currents associated with the Virasoro algebra and Kac-Moody algebra, as well as bosonic and fermionic Virasoro operators. We further demonstrate how these Toda-identities can be utilized to develop a method for determining the correlation functions in the Toda model. We also explore the connection between the Toda Toda-identity and the Ward identities in the Toda model. We then proceed to examine the Toda-identity in the context of primary fields and explore its implications in the Toda model. We also explore the connection between the Toda-identity in the Toda model and the Toda identity in the context of primary fields.
