We introduce Relation GAN, a novel approach that incorporates relation networks into traditional GANs through an optimal transport framework. Our method enables the use of a variety of transportation losses in conjunction with traditional adversarial losses, facilitating the generation of a range of image domains. Notably, our model excels in relation-based learning and can efficiently generate a vast number of synthetic data samples for training model robustness. Our research involves multiple real-world domain adaptation and generation experiments, including unpaired and paired settings, and achieves superior results compared to state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, we apply relation GANs with triplet loss to achieve state-of-the-art results in three main areas: (1) paired domain adaptation, (2) unpaired domain adaptation, and (3) image domain generation.

A novel approach for practical quantum communication over long-distance fiber has been developed through the utilization of twin-field quantum entanglement. This method, dependent on phase-synchronizing the quantum devices, tends to be vulnerable to phase errors which significantly hinder key rate performance. In an effort to mitigate this limitation, our approach eliminates the necessity for phase locking and instead employs light back-back channels to distribute keys in an iterative process, using practical error correction methods to mitigate noise effects. This enhanced method exhibits improved robustness and efficiency compared to conventional methods, with associated simulations demonstrating substantial gains in key rate, particularly under conditions of high noise levels where conventional methods are severely impacted. This breakthrough offers a practical and efficient means of quantum communication over long-distance fiber.

For certain subspaces of Fock and Bergman space linearly independent set collections, the corresponding Toeplitz algebras are established, with the underlying space being determined by a countably infinite set of orthogonal or quasi-orthogonal monomials. As a result, the freedom to choose linearly independent sets leads to a multiplicity of Toeplitz algebras for the same space, with the underlying set of monomials being a key factor. With the aid of the central vision of linearly independent set collections, the structure of Toeplitz algebras for the weighted Bergman space WBAp(μ) can be extended to all μ in the positive Bonny measure family, with the process involving a change in the collection of generators for each μ.

Recent object detection methods using image data have yielded impressive results,
yet a major limitation is the need for a fixed set of object categories and
corresponding annotation data. Researchers have tackled this issue by developing
open-vocabulary object detection techniques utilizing text-based descriptions of
objects instead. However, large collections of text-based annotations are
required for training these methods. In response to this challenge, we introduce
open-vocabulary image-text joint detection, a framework that uses image data and
textual descriptions of objects without needing pre-defined categories or
extra training data. A novel text-based pseudo-labeling approach is proposed to
generate bounding box annotations from web image search results, allowing us to
achieve state-of-the-art results on the COCO and VL-BERT benchmarks.

A young stellar object called S1 in the Rho Ophiuchus cloud exhibits strong emission from ionized, atomic, and photo-dissociation regions. Analyzing the object's surrounding gas using a 2D Potts model, we found that the ionized and atomic regions are separate but the photo-dissociation region and atomic regions overlap. This is consistent with the object's dominant infrared light coming from the ionized and atomic regions. The photo-dissociation region is smaller than previously thought and the calculated ionized to atomic mass ratio is large at 7. This is consistent with the object driving its own ionized and atomic gas, with no significant external ionization required. The object's ionized and atomic regions are not aligned with its mid-infrared emission, suggesting that the observed emission is not just from internal or external radiation but also from self-absorption of the continuum radiation by its dense gas.

The widespread success of Transformer models in natural language tasks has piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable absence in the field is a comprehensive review of Transformer models in computer vision, which is why we create an extensive survey of these models. By reinterpreting vision as a sequence-based task that can be modeled by a Transformer, we can leverage the benefits of advancements in the Transformer architecture. This enables the incorporation of vocabulary and positional encoding, as well as the utilization of self-attention, allowing for the consideration of relationships among pixels and hierarchical representations. This survey provides an in-depth overview of the latest developments in Transformer models for computer vision, covering a range of tasks, including image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, and video analysis. We also explore the importance of attention, reconstruction, and regularization in these models, as well as the efficient application of pre-trained models. By highlighting the benefits and limitations of these models, we identify potential future research directions, such as the development of Transformer-based methods for medical imaging, image denoising, and other critical applications.

Mortality forecasting models built on the discrete-time AR model, particularly the multivariate AR model with common factor characteristics, have shown promise in in-depth mortality analysis and prediction. Researchers within the Mortality Analytics from the University of Nonviable Births have developed a variant of this model, known as the multivariate AR(1) model with cluster-specific and common factors, to investigate mortality connections across gender, geographic region, and country, as well as to explore changes over time. By incorporating a latent common time-varying factor, this model enables the identification of shared mortality patterns, distinguishes individual patterns, and examines how these patterns evolve over time. Using data from 67 countries spanning 40 years, this model effectively captures both short-term and long-term trends. By focusing on latent cluster-specific factors, this method significantly outperforms established models such as Lee-Carter and Cairney in both in-sample and cross-validation forecasts, particularly in longer-term forecasts exceeding 10 years.

The combination of Graph Neural Networks and Neural Architecture Search has enabled automated design of complex high-performing models, but their widespread use remains limited due to lengthy computation times. A key factor contributing to these costs is interference between graphs, caused by previous graphs' features still being stored in current graphs' GNNs. To address this, our research investigates the causes and effects of graph interference in NAS and GNNs. A new benchmark is presented to facilitate comparison and evaluation of methods designed to reduce interference, including the introduction of warm-starts. The results indicate that warm-starts significantly improve model quality and training efficiency, outperforming existing solutions.

Time series data in various scientific disciplines are analyzed and measured. One common technique to extract meaningful data patterns involves the use of features such as autocorrelation, mutual information, and scaling properties. These features serve as data descriptors that can be utilized in multiple areas of science. As these features are interdependent, they need to be filtered to avoid correlations that might misleadingly suggest the presence of complex patterns. We developed the R package "theft" to offer a collection of features for time series analysis. The theft R package is comprised of three categories of features: filtering out redundant features using mutual information, one-way and two-way time series feature selection; providing a set of basic features such as autocorrelation, mean, median, mutual information, scaling properties, and wavelet features; and including functions for superset feature selection, decision tree-based classification, feature selection, and decision making.
In a globally hyperbolic CAT(0) space, the three-dimensional convex geodesic space has a non-empty boundary if and only if it is homeomorphic to the three-dimensional Lobachevsky space.

Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an essential component of professional translation services, enabling the evaluation of a translator's effectiveness and reliability. Traditional TQA relies on a limited framework that focuses on a translator's technical abilities, rather than their overall reliability factors such as consistency, including their use of terminology, style, and overall quality. This study aims to develop a novel, innovative TQA framework grounded in a comprehensive set of reliability indicators, rather than the conventional list-based approach. Furthermore, we sought to incorporate the perspectives of end-users, translators, and clients in establishing the framework. In addition, we drew from existing research in Translation Memory and Risk Management to establish a robust and adaptable framework that could be applied to various domains and languages. This study also explored the feasibility of a Bayesian approach in assessing a translator's reliability based on their performance history, which would facilitate more accurate and data-driven decision-making in the translation industry.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal energy distribution within the system. Recently, a concept known as eigenchannels has emerged to describe this correlation, where each eigenchannel corresponds to a specific optimal channel for maximum energy deposition. This study derives mathematical rules that govern these eigenchannels, providing insights into how they behave in multiple ways. The derived formulas can be used to predict certain properties of these eigenchannels, even when specific input wave patterns are unknown. The validity of these findings is confirmed through numerical simulations. The discovered properties are expected to have significant applications in fields, such as tailored medicine applications and directed energy deposition.

We've found that using pruning methods on artificial neural networks significantly
reduces their size while maintaining their performance, and can even reveal smaller
sub-networks with higher accuracy than their full counterparts. Our study focuses
on understanding the inherent biases of these "lucky network subsets." We looked at
the effects of pruning methods on various architectures, including different sizes of
FCN and CNN layers, and observed a pattern where the pruned sub-networks show a
strong resemblance to the original network in terms of their structure. However, a
closer examination revealed that the pruned sub-networks exhibit distinct
characteristics, such as fewer parameters, reduced variability in neuron outputs,
and more focused features, which are beneficial for tasks like image classification.
Our results suggest that when given the right conditions, such as sufficient data
and an optimal initial model, pruning can help identify a superior sub-network, and
may be used as a tool to improve model design and develop more efficient
pruning techniques in the future.

In lotteries with a large number of tickets, it's rare for the winner to be an undisturbed, unmodified ticket. However, through a process called "distillation," it's possible to find highly valued tickets within partially modified lottery tickets. This is done by selectively removing some ticket components, making the remaining tickets more likely to win. Our research focuses on finding the best way to distill lotteries, and we develop an algorithm that does so by selectively removing groups of tickets. This algorithm uses an estimation of the tickets' values to determine which ones to remove first, and it maximizes the chances of the remaining tickets winning. Our results include upper bounds on the best-possible odds for the modified lottery tickets, and we verify the algorithm's effectiveness using computer simulations.

The large-charge expansion technique relies on the operator-product-expansion method to analyze systems at strong coupling, such as QCD at high charge, where renormalization group behavior is well understood.  A crucial step in this expansion involves determining the anomalous dimension of specific operators used in the analysis.  A key innovation of the large-charge expansion lies in its ability to accurately match operators used in the analysis to those present in the underlying theory.  In this study, the anomalous dimension of a specific $\phi^Q$ operator at six loops was calculated in a theory with $O(N)$ symmetry, building on previous work where the calculation was only done up to five loops.  By calculating the anomalous dimension of this operator, the researchers were able to derive a relation that can be used to test the operators used in the large-charge expansion method.  A related calculation on the two-scalar operator allowed the researchers to verify previously obtained results and identify discrepancies in previous calculations.  Additionally, the researchers were able to use their results to shed light on the behavior of specific systems at strong coupling, such as the $O(N)$ $\lambda\phi^4$ model and the $SU(N)$ QCD with $N_f=2$ and $N_f=8$ quarks.

Our research explores how certain processes, such as angular momentum coupling and charge interaction, affect properties in 2D materials with valley states. We found that these mechanisms, including one that involves coupling between valley states and optical vibrations, can lead to significant changes in behaviors like valley Hall effect and optical vibrations. By modeling this in a 2D graphene-like material, we saw that these mechanisms cause drift currents and new optical effects. However, the effect of charge interaction on conductivity is much weaker compared to the other mechanisms, leading to a return of the Hall effect when a substantial magnetic field is applied.

This paper outlines our winning solution to the Visual Domain Adaptation challenge in the NeurIPS 2022 Domain Adaptation and Translation Tuning competition. Our approach leverages a novel domain adaptation method that utilizes a style transformer, combined with a state-of-the-art efficient transformer-based model, to achieve exceptional results on the dataset provided by the challenge organizers. Our method, which relies heavily on code efficiency and a minimal number of parameters, allows for effective and efficient domain adaptation, ultimately securing first place in the competition. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/jeaes/NeurIPS2022VDA.

t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, assuming Gaussian distributions for nearby points. This assumption isn't applicable to data with bounded ranges, such as that resulting from hyperspheres with positive curvature, which instead follows a von Mises-Fisher distribution. This research presents a straightforward modification to the loss function and gradients in the original probabilistic t-SNE algorithm to accommodate VMF distributions on spherical data. Simulation experiments reveal the modified algorithm yields superior results when data is VMF-distributed and visually effective with data from hyperspheres, such as human brain surface or network representations, and even performs well on unbounded data from the UMI family.

We use the analytical Diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach to investigate the properties of the 2D Fermi polaron at low temperatures and extremely low densities of impurities. The results show that the ground state many-body wave function consists of a single compact diagram with two propagators and two interaction vertices, which has a finite range in the limit of low densities. The analytical Diagrammatic Monte Carlo method yields precise results for the polaron mass, the binding energy of the polaron, and the interaction length, which align with the results from the Second Born approximation in this specific context.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, specific gate realizations can be directly applied to both qubits and qudits, without requiring an intermediate analog processor. We investigate the digital-analog method's suitability for simulating complex many-body fermionic systems using a fermionic Hamiltonian on a 2D square lattice and a 2D Hubbard lattice. We demonstrate that a particular digital gate can efficiently achieve a simulating environment with short-range interactions. This method can be further expanded to include longer-range connections. We also examine the influence of noise on fermionic systems and propose a noise-reducing technique. Our study provides a foundation for applying the digital-analog method to fermionic quantum simulation and related experiments, like fermionic quantum chemistry calculations.

Graph polynomials hold significant value due to their ability to generate graph invariants, which can be utilized to define graph classes through polynomial-based equivalence relations. Certain graph polynomials, such as the Chi-polynomial and Zeta-polynomial, exhibit characteristics of a Galois connection, establishing a connection with symmetric polynomials. This property enables the derivation of algebraic results along with the generation of interesting polynomial sequences. The Chi-polynomial and Zeta-polynomial sequences display similarities with other well-known polynomial sequences, such as the Arf-Kac sequence and the Jacobi-Priestley-Scott polynomial sequence. The generation of these polynomial sequences is shown to be computational, while some of the underlying polynomials are proven to be irreducible.

We derive an expression for the pullback of the Hitchin connection, extending the work of Belolipetsky-Long-Yang and its monodromy representations, to a specific Veech curve associated with a 2-generated Teichmüller curve.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a significant increase in remote work worldwide.
As a result, companies are facing new challenges in managing distributed teams using
agile project management techniques, particularly with home-based teams using
remote working methods like Scrum. Although Scrum is designed for co-location, it
has some adaptive features that allow it to function relatively well in remote settings.
However, there is no conclusive evidence on how home-based Scrum teams perform
compared to co-located ones. Our study aims to fill this knowledge gap by examining
the success of home-based Scrum teams through a quantitative analysis of multiple
data sets combined with qualitative data from a survey. Our findings suggest that
home-based Scrum teams can achieve similar success to co-located ones, but are more
susceptible to difficulties due to distance and technology limitations. Successful home-
based Scrum teams often employ specific strategies like regular video calls and
technology tools to mitigate these challenges. Our study offers practical advice for
home-based Scrum teams to achieve success.

The concept of dichotomous matrices serves as an expanded interpretation of Hermitian matrices, with newly formulated guidelines identifying which arrowhead matrices fit this expanded definition. Furthermore, specific conditions were derived to ensure unitary irreducibility of these expanded matrices, and their maximum orthonormal vector count was calculated in relation to boundary numerical range, a concept related to the Gau-Wu number. In doing so, all numerical range and Gau-Wu number values were calculated for 4x4 arrowhead and Hermittian matrices.

In a study of Pb-Pb collisions at a high energy of 5.02 TeV, researchers examined the elliptical movement of electrons created when beauty particles decay. They used ALICE detector data at the CERN LHC and discovered that electrons moving in an elliptical shape when not moving in the direction of the collision's direction of motion have a higher count. This finding is more common among collisions where particles collided at a specific angle to the direction of motion, and it is more frequent among particles that collided at a higher speed. This suggests that elliptical movement is caused by the way the energy released in the collision moves towards different directions, and it is more frequent among collisions where particles collided at a higher speed and at a specific angle to the direction of motion.

In pursuit of breakthroughs in the medical field, we analyze chromatic configurations in three-dimensional space, employing topological concepts. Leveraging techniques borrowed from image processing, we develop mathematically sound indicators to capture both fine-scale and broad-scale interplay among color categories. Our proposed methods enable fast computation by adapting techniques such as Delaunay tessellations and alpha-shapes for color mapping.

This work focuses on the interference network with $K$ transmitters and receivers where each transmitter employs power control through $2^{[\sqrt{K}]}$ discrete power levels to maximize the sum rate GDoF. To achieve this, we propose a novel, computationally efficient power control scheme that outperforms binary control yet requires minimal design parameters. Notably, the optimal power levels can be determined without explicit knowledge of the network topology, thanks to the use of geometric principles. Furthermore, the power levels can be evenly divided among the transmitters if a centralized controller is present, eliminating the need for individual design parameters. As the number of users increases, the gain in sum rate GDoF over binary power control grows at a rate proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, at least for $K=8$.

Auditing business processes often requires categorization of complex data.
Weighted bipartite graphs can represent transactions between financial entities,
and specialists can translate this data into formal contexts. Formal concept analysis
enables automated extraction of categories based on these contexts, and their
evaluation relies on expertise similar to that required for manual categorization.
Multiple categories may be used simultaneously in auditing, and categorization
resistance analysis can be performed through Dempster-Shafer theory on formal contexts.

The Strauss process is a point process, and its density is unnormalized relative to a Poisson point process, incorporating a weighting factor lambda, between zero and one, which is applied to each pair of points closer than a certain distance, denoted as 'r'. Traditional methods for effficiently simulating the Strauss process are limited, and most rely on Poisson process simulations. However, these methods often result in unnecessary points that are outside the process's effective area. We propose a new method, referred to as'stitching,' which efficiently simulates the Strauss process. This method starts with generating a Poisson process over a larger area, calculating the probability of points within the process's effective area, and then selecting and'stitching' a subset of these points within the area. We've developed an algorithm that utilizes stitching, and through simulations, we've determined that the method is not only highly efficient but also highly accurate in smaller areas, outperforming existing methods.

In the context of string theory and quantum gravity, the Generalized Uncertainty Principle revealed the presence of an inherent minimum length, confirmed through GUP modifications in various quantum systems. The paper investigates how GUP impacts transformations between inertial frames in both Galilean and special relativistic frameworks, focusing on the lattice GUP formulation. For low-energy processes, GUP introduces minimal length corrections in a manner consistent with existing literature. The analysis shows that lattice GUP of order $\hbar/c$ yields accurate results for Lorentz transformations with minimal length corrections, closely approximating established outcomes. The paper provides a comprehensive mathematical framework for GUP corrections in special relativity, demonstrating that lattice GUP effectively predicts precise minimal length corrections in both Galilean and special relativity with minimal length of $\hbar/c$.

Multitasking scheduling in service industries has gained significant attention, and we extend its core assumption that customers arrive one at a time to a more realistic model where multiple customers can be present at any time. Each customer requires a specific service time duration. While the classic model relies solely on service times to determine waiting times and server utilization rates, we develop a more comprehensive approach that allows customers to share processing, yielding new insights into server usage and waiting times. Our method is backed by a distribution-free upper bound, and we outline a procedure for effective planning and control in such systems.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate soft and flexible terrain. Developing an accurate model for leg-terrain interaction, which accounts for force resistance in accordance with the theory of plasticity, can help mitigate this problem. This paper presents an analytical model for a one-legged hopping robot as it moves over deformable ground. To achieve this, a force model based on Coulomb friction with linear elastic resistance is employed, particularly in the direction perpendicular to the ground surface. By simulating the leg's penetration using the theory of plasticity, the model's friction behavior becomes independent of the contact area's size. This results in a total of 14 degrees of freedom for the single-legged robot, which are then optimized using a quadratic programming algorithm in order to execute a hopping motion. To verify the proposed model, the researchers conducted both physical and analytical analyses of the robot's hopping ability, demonstrating good agreement between simulation and reality.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of Internet of Things (IoT) networks, periodic firmware updates are crucial for maintaining optimal network performance and security. Given the escalating complexity of firmware management and the potential risks, it has become increasingly essential to investigate current practices. We conducted an in-depth analysis of the latest wireless mesh networking technologies, focusing on how they implement and execute firmware updates. Our comprehensive study assessed five leading mesh networks: mesh Wi-Fi, Raspbian OS, OpenWRT, Gluon OS, and StarMesh. Our results revealed that Raspbian and OpenWRT excel in terms of efficiency, while Gluon and StarMesh offer improved stability and security. However, Raspbian and OpenWRT consistently delivered the fastest and most reliable update times. We conclude that RaspMesh is the superior choice due to its robustness, high quality, and wide support, outshining Gluon in every aspect despite the latter's added features.

We investigate the properties of the many-body localization phase transition by analyzing the multifractal dimensions of the eigenstates of a one-dimensional spin system. Our results show that the eigenstates have complex fractal structures, and the multifractal dimensions of these eigenstates determine their quantum information content. Additionally, our findings indicate that the eigenstates near the many-body localization threshold have a specific scaling behavior with energy. Our analysis also takes into account the level repulsion effect and is verified by the use of the infinite time-evolving block decimation method to obtain the eigenstates.

This paper presents an interactive search framework designed to locate multiple targets within a terrain, utilizing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unoccupied aerial systems (UASs) that require periodic recharging. To optimize search efficiency, UAVs employ real-time path re-routing based on target proximity and energy levels, while UASs adopt a more conservative approach due to their slower speeds. A decision-making process, facilitated by a probabilistic surface, enables targets to be selected or discarded during an ongoing search, and a case study utilizing Google Earth data highlights the value of targeted information in reducing search time, often up to 50% more efficient than non-targeted approaches.

Researchers have successfully developed universal adversarial examples against traditional machine learning classifiers that process classical data. However, the field of quantum computing remains unexplored in this context. This study aims to fill this gap by creating universal examples of imperceptible changes and malicious inputs that can deceive quantum classifiers based on classical neural networks, regardless of the input data. Additionally, a universal set of modifications that can fool these quantum classifiers for any given input has been discovered.

We examine Steklov eigenvalues in nearly spherical domains of three dimensions.  Building on our earlier research, which demonstrated the eigenvalues to be analytic functions of domain perturbation, we show that in the Steady-State case, these eigenvalues are approximately analytic up to the second order in domain perturbation.  We further derive formulas for their derivatives, specifically in terms of harmonic coordinates in the domain.  These findings have practical implications for nearly spherical domains.  We illustrate our results for a domain shaped like a sphere except at its top, where we join the unit disk.  Similar conclusions apply to domains shaped like a sphere except at its bottom, where we join the half-ball.  We also show that conclusions about analytical properties can be extended to nearly confocal disk eigenvalues and the incompressible fluid flow outside a disk with a small hole.

Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process models and observed process behavior. However, alignments can be computationally expensive and inefficient for large datasets. To address performance issues and limit memory usage, this research introduces a new technique that analyzes smaller sections of data at a time. The technique, named Infix Postfix Alignments, is tested and shown to be more efficient than traditional alignments, effectively handling larger datasets and reducing memory usage.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are often insufficient due to the increasing complexity of modern networks and their inherent limitations. Leveraging recent advances in machine learning, particularly in image analysis, we present a novel deep learning approach to predict downlink path loss with remarkable results. Compared to conventional models and deep learning methods, our model achieves the highest level of accuracy, effectively generalizing to new scenarios. Its high accuracy is due to its ability to generate reliable predictions even with limited data and adapt to diverse network configurations and environments.

A straightforward semantics is proposed for temporal planning. We define and formally establish the logic within the interactive theorem prover Isabelle/HOL and also demonstrate that a widely employed practical implementation of temporal planning adheres to this semantics. By using the established practical implementation based on the established semantics, validation becomes a straightforward process for verifying individual plans against the given problem's specifications. We have successfully proven and validated the correctness of three sample temporal plans in the practical setting used.

Power system expansion planning models are crucial for determining optimal siting of generation, transmission, and energy storage facilities in the long-term. These plans aim to satisfy expected power demand and meet system reliability requirements at minimum cost, incorporating considerations for renewable energy integration, climate change, and environmental sustainability. These plans are particularly important for utilities planning to transition to low-carbon energy systems, incorporating emerging technologies such as flexible AC lines and modular energy storage facilities. However, the inherent complexity and approximations in these planning models may result in suboptimal solutions and conflicting recommendations for actual power system operations. This study assesses the robustness of power system expansion planning models by comparing solutions generated using different models, assumptions, and scenarios. The results indicate that the output of these models is highly dependent on the specific model used, key parameters, and scenario assumptions. Furthermore, the models may overlook critical power system characteristics and fail to provide viable solutions for actual operational purposes.

This study establishes global existence for solutions of the relativistic Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation. Furthermore, under non-reflection boundary conditions for the Vlasov equation, we prove the existence of long-term solutions for the non-relativistic Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models.

When performing code analysis, developers often struggle to pinpoint the relevant section of code as they navigate through their program's execution sequence. To streamline this process, researchers have developed search term identification techniques that can optimize search terms for code navigation. Current approaches, however, rely on developers' prior knowledge and involve manually crafting search terms based on program execution traces. To address this issue, our proposed system automatically generates search terms from developers' prior knowledge and execution traces, making code analysis more efficient. The system's search terms were tested on a dataset and compared to existing methods, revealing its effectiveness in locating relevant code sections efficiently.

Researchers have discovered a novel method to modify the mechanical and flow properties of colloidal gels by introducing ultrasonic vibrations. By subjecting the gels to these high-frequency vibrations, the solid colloidal network becomes disrupted, enabling the gel to transition into a more fluid state that can flow more easily. This rheological transformation is not influenced by changes in temperature, making ultrasonic vibrations a highly controllable and efficient means to alter the gel's properties. Interestingly, the gel's new state exhibits characteristics of non-Newtonian behavior with a viscosity that relies on the rate of shear and pressure applied. An advanced model that incorporates the effects of ultrasonic vibrations has been developed, successfully explaining the observed changes in the gel's behavior. This research opens up new possibilities for manipulating the properties of colloidal gels and other complex materials using high-frequency sound waves.

This research paper investigates the Collatz conjecture, also known as the 3x+1 problem. This theory posits that given any positive integer starting value, repeated applications of a specific transformation (tripping off the odd number and doubling the even number) will eventually yield a value of 1. To explore this idea, we examine the properties of the function f(n) = 3n for odd n and 2n for even n, and consider the sequence of numbers generated by this function. By analyzing the behavior of this sequence, we look at the number of steps required to reach 1 as a function of the initial value, and explore how this count changes as the initial value grows. In the process, we establish some key results about the behavior of this function and prove them.

To effectively organize digital collections and facilitate targeted searching within a particular field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial. In fields like Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics, specific keywords and phrasings can significantly impact a paper's understanding by specialists in the same field. Notwithstanding the significance of subject classification in STEM fields, current techniques face challenges due to the highly specialized nature of textual content and dominantly technical content. This work proposes a novel approach to tackle this problem by integrating a mathematical entity detection system to extract crucial information from STEM papers' full-text content and improve classification results. Our proposed approach was tested on a large dataset and showed a substantial increase in its classification accuracy compared to existing methods.

The classic stable marriage problem involves finding suitable matches between members of two groups, provided their initial preferences align. In its proposed version, two agents from different groups take turns suggesting matches until one is successfully accepted. This paper examines the conditions under which the existing algorithms guarantee that the agents will find a suitable match. It is demonstrated that requiring only a subset of agents to initiate proposals, chosen either randomly or based on specific criteria, is insufficient to ensure a match is found. However, if algorithms are allowed to select agents to make proposals in response to their previous actions, things change. In particular, if agents are chosen uniformly at random, or if selection is made with the goal of finding a match, such as through a potential matching forecaster, these algorithms ensure that the resulting matches are stable. Furthermore, if agents are allowed to stop proposing once they think a match is imminent, such as through a prediction based on their previous actions, these algorithms achieve nearly the same efficiency as existing algorithms.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization models are inadequate, as they often contradict human judgments of summary quality. To address this, a new evaluation system called SummScore is proposed, designed to assess the overall quality of a summary by measuring its semantic similarity to the original text. Unlike existing metrics that solely focus on coherence or accuracy, SummScore provides a comprehensive assessment of summary quality, distinguishing between text cohesiveness, relevance, and overall quality. Furthermore, SummScore can serve as a strong baseline performance metric due to its ability to accurately predict human ratings. To achieve this, a high-performance pre-trained CrossEncoder model is fine-tuned using human-annotated summary datasets. Additionally, a novel technique is introduced to train the CrossEncoder without supervision, leveraging pre-existing summary datasets without requiring human annotation. Overall, SummScore is a versatile and adaptable evaluation metric that can be easily customized to assess specific summary qualities by adjusting its training objectives.

A new method for extracting a sparse signal from cross-related data is presented, outperforming existing techniques both computationally and in terms of recovery accuracy. This type of correlated data is typical in various fields such as magnetoresistance measurement, radioastronomical observation etc. The proposed technique relies on leveraging the underlying matrix's eigenvalue distribution, thereby requiring no a-priori knowledge of the signal's characteristics. The method's recovery performance is guaranteed as long as the ratio of signal strength to noise exceeds a certain threshold, which can be precisely determined. The method's simplicity and efficiency are further highlighted through its low computational requirements for large datasets, as demonstrated through its implementation in Python.

The widespread use of LiDAR and high-resolution cameras in autonomous vehicles and robotic platforms has led to significant advancements in 3D object detection. However, the need for synchronized data from both sensors is a significant limitation. Various data synthesis and fusion methods have been developed to address this issue, with 3D-ray tracing and camera-LiDAR fusion being the most prominent approaches. In particular, the problem of false positives caused by LiDAR noise and camera reflections in PCL-based fusion methods is a major concern. This paper presents BEVFusion, a novel camera-LiDAR fusion method that leverages event cameras and 3D-ray tracing for enhanced accuracy and robustness. By utilizing event cameras, the proposed method can accurately detect intense changes in the environment and adapt to various event-camera formats. Moreover, the integration of LiDAR data eliminates the need for 3D data reconstruction from camera data, making BEVFusion a more efficient and robust solution. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of BEVFusion compared to existing PCL-based fusion methods, with a notable increase of up to 11.3% in AP$_{50}$ and 6.5% in AP$_{75}$ and an average reduction of 10.0% in false positives.

We're investigating the interaction between the collective behavior of particles and thermal fluctuations in a fluid under extreme conditions, far from its natural state. By employing a multi-scale approach, we explore how these fluctuations impact the fluid's behavior, from its dissipation range up to 100 times its dissipation scale, and compare our results to laboratory observations of similar scenarios in geophysical fluids. Our analysis reveals that at this scale, the fluid's behavior is dominated by the non-linear effects of turbulence and the effects of thermal fluctuations, particularly in relation to energy transfer. We've developed a theoretical model that accounts for these fluctuations and their impact on the fluid's behavior, and our results suggest that these fluctuations could significantly modify our understanding of geophysical fluids, potentially opening new avenues for research in these complex systems.

Previous studies on laser propagation through a heated fluid employed simplified thermal conductivity and convective heat transfer assumptions, leading to inaccurate predictions. This study presents an in-depth numerical analysis of laser energy absorption and heat distribution, along with the resulting diffraction patterns, in a heated fluid with non-uniform temperature. The study examined both heat diffusion and convection but found the latter to be more rapid. The study shows that as the laser interacts with the fluid, its energy is initially absorbed uniformly across the beam, before diffusion and convective heat transport distort the intensity, causing the laser beam to spread and change phase. The study explains the observed complex diffraction patterns, including multiple dark bands, as a result of heat diffusion and convective effects.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including technical exchanges, social encounters, and reflections on code.  A key aspect of satellite meetings associated with a programming conference consists of various group discussions regarding open source software development, encompassing DDDs.  To facilitate the mining of DDDs for their design content, a model called ConStMDDM was introduced in 2021.  By applying ConStMDDM to a dataset of DDDs from the International Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering, it was found that design content stability in DDDs is relatively low.  A comparison of ConStMDDM with statistical and machine learning methods revealed that it is the most effective model for capturing the stability of design content in DDDs.  Furthermore, it was discovered that design content in DDDs is stable when compared to other forms of programming discussions, but unstable when compared to group design meetings.  Ultimately, the success of ConStMDDM suggests that it may be useful for other purposes, such as classifying DDDs according to their subtopics.

This paper presents a novel approach to stream processing that enables the querying and analysis of both real-time and historical data, while ensuring seamless integration and consistency. Our method addresses the issue of stream-based querying by representing these streams as hypergraphs, allowing us to adaptively adjust the hypergraph structure as needed. In addition, we leverage hypergraphs to store historical data, enabling efficient analysis and mining capabilities. Our proposed technique, H-STREAM, serves as a stream processing engine that manages hypergraphs to facilitate the analysis and querying of both real-time and historical data. H-STREAM's key features include hypergraph management, stream processing, and query handling, along with a physical storage layer to support these capabilities. Our approach is validated through various analytical pipelines, demonstrating H-STREAM's effectiveness in tackling complex data analysis tasks.

The hunt for Top and Bottom companions is a significant area of study in Beyond the Standard Model theories, particularly through single production reactions. In this study, the impact of non-resonant diagrams on single production Top and Bottom partner cross-sections has been examined, revealing that non-resonant contributions can be substantial, up to 30%, and are particularly significant at large quark momentum. By comparing the Standard Model and various models beyond the Standard Model, including both weak and flavor universal theories, the study established criteria for resonant dominance and non-resonant dominance, and found that non-resonant contributions can be observed experimentally at the LHC with significantly lower luminosity than previously thought, down to 100 fb^-1.

In recent years, the SPARQL query translation problem has garnered significant interest, with several approaches developed to tackle it. However, many of these solutions are hindered by their inability to effectively utilize knowledge base elements, specifically when dealing with a large number of subjects, predicates, and objects. To address this limitation, our proposed solution employs a copy mechanism for subjects, predicates, and objects to enable selective retrieval of relevant elements from the knowledge base during translation. By incorporating a specialized element extractor that leverages element presence and relevance to guide copy mechanism usage, our approach further improves performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing solutions, with particular improvements in handling elements with sparse data.

This work introduces a novel method for systematically evaluating the quality of individual journals and conferences based on the performance of their published papers. Our model evaluates each venue by how effectively it enhances the career advancement of its authors through its research publications, providing a quantitative score for each venue that accounts for factors like career stage, publication fields, and performance standards. Our approach, known as Venue Analytics, leverages large-scale data and is highly adaptable, allowing for easy expansion to various domains with minimal adjustments. By analyzing a substantial dataset of papers and their corresponding career outcomes, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Venue Analytics, showcasing its differences with traditional metrics like impact factors and citation analysis.

Advanced learning methods can address long-standing challenges in control, but their predictive models are often difficult to assess or verify mathematically. In this paper, a framework is introduced to establish the formal verification of control systems using deep neural networks. It initially addresses verification of state constraints by converting a related control problem into a proven robustness issue for safety-critical neural networks. Subsequently, a key result in this area is utilized to develop an efficient method for this transformation, enabling the use of established algorithms for verifying neural networks. This approach is then extended to include verification of input constraints. Numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, especially when traditional tools are inadequate. Finally, the potential areas of application and limitation of this approach are discussed.

This study offers two novel clustering algorithms that cater to real-world data, 
addressing limitations in existing methods. The algorithms ensure a hierarchical 
structure, allowing for cluster overlaps and functorial properties. The first 
algorithm, based on the principle of minimum spanning trees, provides a time 
efficient clustering method. The text outlines computational proofs of the 
algorithm's correctness. The second method uses a dynamic information distance 
and results in a time efficient clustering, overlapping or not. The text includes 
comparisons of these algorithms through experimental evaluation with standard 
clustering techniques.

Tensor completion has become a crucial method for recovering incomplete and noisy data, particularly effective in visual data recovery, but it faces challenges in efficient processing, especially with large datasets and real-time applications. Recent advancements in streaming tensor recovery for incomplete data processing have drawbacks, such as extended latency and increased hardware demands. In response, a new approach, patch tracking-based streaming tensor recovery, is developed to provide efficient and effective data recovery with reduced latency and improved performance. This innovative method integrates patch tracking and tensor recovery techniques, utilizing patch-based updates to facilitate efficient and real-time data recovery. Initial results demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of this approach, offering a promising solution for streaming tensor recovery.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ take the form of type D. This finding has implications for Nichols algebras associated with irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_{n}$, revealing that these algebras have infinite dimensions, with the exception of three distinct cases: the $(2, 3),(1^{2}, 3)$ case in $\mathbb S_{5}$, and the $(1^{n-2}, 2)$ case in $\mathbb S_{n}$ for $n >5$.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been found to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box of various resolutions to model turbulent flows, which they then analyzed via Fourier-Ganesh transform to test for scale-invariant energy distributions. Notably, when accounting for effects of viscous friction and finite box sizes, the researchers found that their model satisfied the requirements of a scale-invariant energy cascade according to the famous Kolmogorov spectrum, which describes a unique, universal frequency distribution in turbulent flows.

Researchers have been exploring deep learning models that utilize graph neural networks (GNNs) to solve graph-based problems efficiently. A recent model, iterative graph normalization (IGN), has gained attention for its ability to learn graph representations by transforming input graphs into a maximum weight independent set (MWIS) sequence. However, IGN's performance relies heavily on the properties of random matrices, which are often derived from edge weights. As a result, IGN may not be suitable for tasks requiring robustness against varying conditions. In response, this study proposes an alternative method, called iterative graph normalization with sigma-zeros (IGNSZ), which supplements IGN with sigma-zeros. By adding columns of known zeros to the derivative matrix, IGNSZ ensures that its robustness and performance are not compromised by the standard deviation of the input graphs. In addition to providing a detailed explanation of IGN and IGNSZ, this study also includes a comprehensive evaluation of their effectiveness, including comparisons with alternative models on various graph-based tasks.

This research studies the impact of a magnetic field on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, aiming to understand the effect of a periodic potential on the thermodynamic properties of this material.
By analyzing the Landau levels in electrically modulated graphene, we determined the interplay between the applied electric field and magnetic field on the density of states.
Based on this analysis, we calculated the magnetic susceptibility and specific heat as functions of temperature and magnetic field.
Our computations revealed that the periodic potential elevates the magnetic susceptibility and specific heat above their counterparts in normal single-layer graphene.
Furthermore, we found that the periodic potential introduces a magnetic field-induced phase transition, as evidenced by a discontinuity in the magnetic susceptibility at a specific critical magnetic field strength.

Recent findings from ongoing monitoring campaigns of low-frequency radio emission from systems containing an active flare star reveal a distinctive pattern in CR Draconis. Continuous, non-thermal radio emission emanating from the system can be attributed to an electron-cyclotron maser instability triggered by magnetospheric plasma oscillations. A notable 10-year pattern in CR Draconis emerges, with periods of increased radio activity lasting around 7.8 years and alternating with relatively quiet periods, despite thorough analysis that rules out any correlation with the rotational sampling of the star and planet magnetic fields. This is accompanied by a notable 7.5-year periodicity in the binary orbit of CR Draconis, indicating a possible link between the star and planet magnetic field configurations. Moreover, radio emission in CR Draconis is found to be consistently polarized in the north-south direction, with a polarization fraction that can reach up to 100%. In contrast, radio emission from the individual stars in the binary system is not detectable, suggesting that the radio emission is not generated by the individual stars themselves but rather by the shared magnetospheric plasma. This is further supported by observations of another binary system containing active flare stars, with radio emission detected only when both stars are observable and not when the stars are in occultation.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for a large number of transformation matrices - 78 for a typical human body model.
To address this, our new method employs a single transformer layer to map key bones
to keyframe rotations and then uses standard bone weighting to determine each
point's rotation. We present ANR, a method that combines mesh representations with
neural rendering, resulting in photorealistic, dynamically posed avatar images.
Given only a static model, ANR enables the creation of avatars that can be posed
realistically using any animation system, even one not originally designed with
neural techniques.

We investigate how much variations in image presentation affect human and machine learning performance across different domains. To address this, we created a tool that alters images in a way that optimizes them for a specific task while maintaining their original identity. When applied to tasks such as facial recognition, the transformed images become near indistinguishable from each other, yet still depict the same individual. We examine the impact of these transformations on both machine learning models and the average human performer across multiple fields, including visual recognition, object detection, and text analysis. Our results show that machines are more susceptible to these image transformations than humans, with performance often dropping by half or more. We discover that certain methods like data augmentation and image enhancement methods are less effective in addressing these transformations. We also find that humans and machines respond differently to these transformations at different stages of processing, with visual perception being particularly vulnerable. Our work has practical applications and raises important questions about how these transformations impact performance in real-world scenarios.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory, along with its relationship to the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant, which uses quantum algebra $U_q(so_2)$, is explored in this study. It's observed that certain fusion channels of interest in the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory can be represented by the generators of the Askey-Wilson algebra. Utilizing the Turaev-Lackenbach theorem, which establishes a link between the Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariants and orthogonal polynomials, it's found that the Askey-Wilson algebra underlies both the quantum group $U_q(so_2)$ and the associated link invariants. This relationship between the Askey-Wilson algebra and both the SU(2) Chern-Simons theory and Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariants provides new insights into the interplay between quantum groups, Chern-Simons theory, and link invariants.

Our research presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation method, applied to two-dimensional arrays of strongly-connected clusters, interacting with each other via weak inter-cluster bonds. We investigate the ground state properties and thermal behavior of the $\kappa$-LGO and Kitaev materials, which are two-dimensional trimer antifermagentic systems. Through extensive numerical simulations, we calculated the magnetic energy, spin freezing behavior, and entanglement in Kitaev models with different $\kappa$-LGO modifications. These calculations were performed for various strength of inter-cluster connections, ranging from weak to strong. We also identified the critical temperature at which three-dimensional spin freezing occurs in the Kitaeb-LGO model, and compared it to the simulation results for a Kitaeb model with randomly placed impurities. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the Kitaeb-LGO model exhibits a finite ground-state entropy similar to Kitaeb models with large clusters, and that this value decreases as inter-cluster connections strengthen. However, if connections are limited to nearest neighbors, the simulation reveals an exponential divergence of entanglement at a transition temperature that can be accurately predicted using a modified analytical formula derived from a perturbative model of weakly-coupled clusters.

Pre-trained language models, when given appropriate prompts, can perform various tasks such as natural language translation, question-answering, and image description. To achieve this, researchers have been exploring different learning strategies and datasets to enable pre-trained models to perform tasks outside their original training scope. A dataset and prompt collection, Meta-Learn-CC, has been developed to facilitate this process. The collection includes 34 datasets, 15 prompts, and associated metadata, allowing for a large-scale analysis of pre-trained models under new learning conditions. By using Meta-Learn-CC, researchers found that model fine-tuning on multiple datasets and prompts simultaneously leads to improved zero-shot learning performance, and that model size and pre-training time have a direct impact on this achievement. The collection and accompanying findings are published to facilitate further research into zero-shot learning.

The investigation into the possibility of a first-order electroweak phase transition in the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM has been initiated. By analyzing the LSP's composition, it was discovered that only the LSP can be a dark matter candidate if it consists of a nearly degenerate set of $N_1$ states. However, this set of states cannot be the sole component of the electroweak vacuum's energy density at the CMB's recombination epoch, as it would lead to an underabundance of the CMB. This limitation arises due to the $Z_3$ symmetry's invariance, as the $N_1$-Higgsino component cannot contribute to the vacuum energy. It was also found that the CMB constraints on the CMB's energy power spectrum can be satisfied with a CMB relaxation scale of approximately $10^{11}$ GeV or larger. This relaxation scale is not a part of the model's parameters. This investigation also revealed that the CMB's energy power spectrum's amplitude is determined by the CMB's relaxation scale's logarithm's magnitude, as well as the CMB's phase. This relationship was found to be independent of the CMB's temperature. We introduce novel approaches for identifying robust redshifts in abundance matching and demographic models, focusing on dusty galaxy populations detected at redshifts exceeding z=4 through millimeter or submillimeter spectroscopy or photometry. By employing a detailed, pseudo-observed data panel, we demonstrate the effectiveness of various redshift indicators and how some, such as a specific Lyman break galaxy feature, can be used at redshifts where previously no robust indicators existed. We identify specific spectral features and break points that can be used as redshift indicators and show that a combination of these can be combined into a "panda" function, allowing for an easy visual identification of robust and relatively robust redshifts. This "High-z Sudoku" technique enables researchers to efficiently rule out or identify specific models based on their predicted redshift distributions and can be used for both individual objects and broader population models.

We conducted extensive time-evolving simulations on a half-spinned triangular lattice system to investigate the emergence of symmetry-breaking and liquid phases following a quench from the fully polarized state. By analyzing the spin structure factor and correlations at different length scales, we found that the symmetry-breaking phase exhibits characteristic signatures including short-range order and specific long-wavelength fluctuations, whereas the liquid phases are characterized by increasing fluctuations with wavelength. These findings align with theoretical predictions from quantum Monte Carlo simulations.

A $SU(3)$ gauge theory with an $SU(3)$ Higgs field, characterized by a specific set of Lagrangian parameters, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, is studied in this report. By considering the theory in four-dimensional complex space, with complex values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, we can analyze the finite temperature finite density effects on the phase transition in the $SU(3)-$Higgs theory, as described by lattice simulations with an account of the back reaction of the thermal plasma on the Higgs field.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure similar to Mn$_2$Au and is of interest in spintronics due to its ability to order magnetically at high temperatures. This study focused on growing Cr$_2$Al crystals and utilizing neutron diffraction to reveal the in-plane magnetic arrangement and inverting the existing structural model. Furthermore, the findings from neutron pair-distribution function measurements were utilized to determine the exchange interactions in Cr$_2$Al.

A new kinetic model, specifically designed to incorporate variable collision frequencies based on velocity, has been developed and tested against Monte Carlo simulations. This model accounts for rarefied gas flow behavior by modifying the collision frequency in accordance with the intermolecular potential, thereby allowing for the analysis of its influence on rarefied gas flow solutions. Results indicate that the kinetic model's accuracy improves when the collision frequency is matched to the average frequency of molecular interactions in the Monte Carlo simulation.

Building on the 'that'-relation framework, this research explores natural language parsing by shifting from formalized meaning to more organic, meaning-rich representations. A new parser, called NSP, is developed to generate these more abstract interpretations. Rather than relying on formalized semantic representations, NSP's focus on capturing the underlying conceptual structure of a sentence, independent of its specific wording. NSP's performance was tested in experiments with a dataset of sentences describing physical world interactions and demonstrated conceptually richer interpretations and superior accuracy in processing these sentences. Additionally, our study shows that NSP's natural language abilities can be effectively fine-tuned even with limited available data.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To achieve precise measurements of deep-inelastic scattering, forward detectors must complement existing detectors and ensure complete coverage of ep and eA collisions in the very forward regions. To meet this goal, advanced forward detectors will be integrated into the existing RHIC detector framework, incorporating cutting-edge technologies to provide detailed three-dimensional tracking at polar angles below 20 degrees. Development of forward silicon detectors is currently underway, with prototype testing in progress using the RHIC accelerator at Brookhaven. We will present the latest developments in forward detector development and show how forward silicon detectors will contribute to our understanding of QCD phenomena, with a focus on the results from recent SiDard prototype testing.

We conducted a detailed study of the low luminosity active galactic nucleus, SDSS J015957 085435, using multiple wavelength observations over its variability period. Our analysis indicates that the source exhibits a complex behavior, characterized by a time scale of variability that matches both the size of the source and the speed of sound in its environment. Furthermore, the source's variability is consistent with the presence of a rotating disk and a varying accretion rate, rather than the influence of a binary black hole. However, the observed outburst of the source also raises questions about the nature of the source's variability, with the possibility of the outburst being a rare event that occurs in low luminosity active galactic nuclei.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. A key aspect of this is the circulation of material within a star's convective zones, with certain theories suggesting that this circulation could transfer magnetic fields from the interior to the exterior of the star. However, the impact of these fields on the formation of spectral lines and the distribution of magnetic fields in a star's atmosphere is still a topic of ongoing research. 

A study of the early B-type star HD58260, known for its strong magnetic field and rapid rotation, has provided new insights into the distribution of magnetic fields in a star's atmosphere. Using advanced spectroscopic techniques, the study has directly measured the gradient of magnetic fields in HD58260, with the fields increasing by approximately 50% over a 200,000 km distance. 

The results of this study are consistent with the idea that turbulent movements in a star's convective zones may transfer magnetic fields from the interior to the exterior of the star. However, further research is needed to confirm this theory and understand the distribution of magnetic fields in a star's atmosphere. 

A comprehensive model of a star's magnetic field, incorporating the transfer of magnetic fields from the interior to the exterior of the star, has been developed. A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

Using ALMA's H30α observations of the metal-poor dwarf galaxy NGC 5253, we calculated the galaxy's star formation rate (SFR) and surface density using different methods. The H30α emission provides a more extensive SFR measurement than optical and near-infrared data, as it includes more information on the galaxy's SFR distribution. The Hα+Hβ, Hα(85.4 μm), and infrared continuum SFR metrics were compared with those derived from H30α and other radio lines. The Hα+Hβ and Hα(85.4 μm) SFR metrics were found to be lower than the H30α SFR metric by a factor of 1.6 and 2.2, respectively. The Hα+Hβ SFR metric overestimated the H30α SFR metric due to the Hα+Hβ SFR metric's sensitivity to the SFR distribution. The Hα(85.4 μm) SFR metric was less sensitive to the SFR distribution, resulting in a more accurate comparison with the H30α SFR metric. The Hα(85.4 μm) SFR metric was also compared with the infrared continuum SFR metric, with the Hα(85.4 μm) SFR metric being 0.4 dex lower than the HFR SFR metric.
